conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. __ from the surgery team. I hear you’re back with abdominal pain and vomiting. Can you tell me what happened today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was fine after I got home, eating okay, sugars were in the 100s. Then I woke up with this constant pain right at my G-tube site and it shoots to my left side. Every time I try to eat, I throw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fevers or chills? Any blood in the vomit or black stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. No blood. Just nausea and vomiting and the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are your bowel movements—any constipation, diarrhea, or not passing gas?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No big change. I’m passing gas. I just can’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: On exam, the area is tender but I don’t see redness, swelling, or drainage around the tube. Your vitals and initial labs look reassuring so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt so much? I’m scared something is leaking again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand the worry, especially with your prior scans and the ulcer irritation at the connection site. Tonight, we’ll treat this conservatively: nothing by mouth for now, IV fluids, and nausea and pain control while we watch closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I’m not eating, won’t my sugar crash?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We’ll check your blood sugar regularly while you’re here, and the IV fluids will help keep you hydrated. If your glucose trends low, we can adjust the fluids and treat it quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you do something for the nausea right now? I feel like I’m going to vomit again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—let’s start with ondansetron, and we can add another medication like prochlorperazine if needed. We’ll also vent the G-tube to release any built-up air or stomach contents and see if that eases the pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Venting it won’t mess it up? I’m worried it’s blocked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do it gently and check that it’s patent. Right now it appears unobstructed, and venting is a common way to relieve nausea and discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The nausea is a little better after the medicine, but the pain is still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll use acetaminophen first and reserve stronger liquid pain medication only if you need it. We want to control pain but also avoid worsening nausea or constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Overnight, your labs stayed within normal limits. We also got chest and abdominal X-rays—no free air and no signs of obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing is wrong? Then why am I vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The imaging rules out some dangerous causes like perforation or a clear blockage. It doesn’t always show irritation or functional issues. Given your history of ulcerations and gastritis, we’re going to keep your stomach-protective meds going—pantoprazole and sucralfate—and keep treating symptoms while we reintroduce intake slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have water at least?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we can start with small sips and see how you do. If you tolerate that, we’ll advance your diet later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I kept down some sips, but I’m scared to eat. Last time it set everything off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We’ll go stepwise—clear liquids first, then something bland. We’ll keep the G-tube clamped if you’re comfortable, and we can vent it again if nausea builds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the tube in the right place? It was exchanged recently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Based on what we’ve seen and how it functions when we vent it, it appears to be in place and not blocked. If symptoms persist, we can get more detailed imaging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I ate a little and didn’t throw up, but the pain near the tube still comes and goes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress on the vomiting. For the pain, we’ll keep using non-NSAID options since you’re allergic and NSAIDs can worsen ulcers. We’ll also keep nausea meds available as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How was your night? Any vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting overnight. I’m still nauseated sometimes, but the zofran helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Today we’ll advance your diet a bit more if you’re willing, and we’ll resume your home medications. We’ll keep checking your blood sugars—so far they’ve stayed in a safe range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about going home and ending up right back here again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a real concern. Our goal is to make sure you can keep food down, your pain and nausea are controlled with oral meds, and your sugars stay stable with your usual routine before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do you think this is from the ulcer area again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be irritation at the gastrogastric connection where you’ve had small clean-based ulcers and gastritis seen on endoscopy before. That’s why we’re emphasizing acid suppression with pantoprazole and coating with sucralfate. But we also want to be sure there isn’t another cause, especially since you’re having recurrent admissions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What else could it be?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes it’s inflammation around the surgical connections, irritation from the tube site, or functional stomach emptying issues. If symptoms don’t keep improving, we’ll get a CT scan to look for abscess, obstruction, or anything acute.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning, you look more comfortable. How’s the pain and nausea now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better than when I came in. I still feel sore around the tube, and I’m nervous to eat full meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep meals small and frequent. The nutrition team will also check in—what matters is whether you’re meeting enough of your calorie needs by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need tube feeds again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now we’re holding tube feeds because they seemed to worsen symptoms before, and you’ve been able to take food by mouth. If you can consistently meet your needs orally and sugars stay stable, we can avoid restarting feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My anxiety is really bad when the pain spikes. I keep thinking something is being missed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry it’s been so stressful. We’ll keep you updated step by step. It’s also okay to use your as-needed anxiety medication if you need it, and we’ll make sure your depression and anxiety meds are continued.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had intermittent pain and nausea despite some improvement, so we’re going to get a CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis with contrast today to look for any acute cause like obstruction or a collection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the CT safe with my tube and all the surgery I’ve had?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The scan will help us see the anastomoses and confirm the G-tube position. You’ll drink oral contrast and also get IV contrast, and we’ll monitor you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried it’s going to show a leak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If there were a leak or abscess, we’d act quickly. The good news is your vitals and labs have stayed stable, which makes a major leak less likely, but the CT will give us more confidence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I have your CT results. It shows normal-appearing surgical connections without evidence of obstruction, and the G-tube balloon is appropriately positioned in the stomach. There’s no abscess or other abnormality to explain the nausea and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s normal… but I still feel it. What does that mean for me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means we’re not seeing anything dangerous that needs surgery right now. The plan is to keep managing this conservatively—control nausea, protect the stomach lining, and focus on steady oral intake while we work on longer-term outpatient strategies for the recurrent pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If tonight goes well—no vomiting, pain controlled with oral meds, and you’re eating enough—then yes, discharge tomorrow is reasonable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I’m still tender, but I’m not throwing up. Zofran is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. The dietitian reviewed your intake, and it looks like you’re taking in more than 75% of what you need by mouth. Your blood sugars have also stayed in normal limits during this stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t need tube feeds at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We’re keeping the tube in place, but you can keep it clamped. If you feel bloated or nauseated, you can vent it as you were taught. We’ll continue to reassess as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my sugar plan? I’m scared of hypoglycemia if I’m eating small amounts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stick with the plan you were given: small frequent low-glycemic meals, protein-based snacks, and check glucose before meals and at bedtime, and more often if you have symptoms or before driving. Keep using your Dexcom to watch trends.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds am I going home on for this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue pantoprazole twice a day and sucralfate four times a day to protect the stomach. You’ll have oral ondansetron for nausea as needed. For pain, acetaminophen first, and a small amount of liquid oxycodone only if pain is severe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the marinol? That helped my appetite last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue dronabinol twice a day since it supports appetite and helps you meet your calorie needs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When should I worry and come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back or call urgently if you can’t keep liquids down, have worsening abdominal pain that doesn’t respond to meds, fever or chills, blood in vomit or stool, black stools, or if your sugars are repeatedly low and not responding to treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m also worried this is going to be my life—pain, admissions, and anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. The CT being reassuring helps us focus on outpatient management—stomach protection, nutrition strategies, and follow-up with your surgical team and dietitian. We’ll also make sure your mental health medications continue and that you have support, because the stress of recurrent symptoms is real.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, can you repeat back the main plan—diet, glucose checks, and meds—so I know it’s clear?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Small frequent low-glycemic meals, protein snacks, check sugars before meals and bedtime and use my Dexcom. Keep the tube clamped but vent if needed. Take pantoprazole and sucralfate, use zofran for nausea, Tylenol first for pain and only a little oxycodone if I really need it. And keep my follow-up appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll discharge you home now. Please take it easy for the next few days and reach out if symptoms flare.
